message.abstract: <jats:p>The valuation of publicly traded software-as-a-service firms depends on how revenue expansion translates into profitability and enterprise value, making the growth–profitability trade-off important for corporate finance, investment analysis, and market valuation. Existing research offers limited evidence on whether the Rule of 40 has the same valuation relevance across development stages when its growth and profitability components are examined separately. This study assesses how revenue growth and earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization margin, independently and jointly, are associated with annual enterprise value growth across revenue-defined groups and whether the Rule of 40 provides a consistent valuation-related indicator. The analysis uses a balanced panel of 30 software-as-a-service companies publicly traded on the United States capital market, with source data covering 2018–2024 and 180 firm-year observations analyzed for 2019–2024; firms are assigned to three fixed groups according to 2018 revenue. The empirical design combines Pearson correlations, pooled and group-specific linear regressions, interaction modelling, median-based growth–profitability profiling, Rule-of-40 quartiles, a binary comparison based on the conventional 40-point benchmark, and 1st/99th percentile winsorization of enterprise value growth. Firm-clustered standard errors with finite-sample correction are used for the principal full-sample regressions. Revenue growth showed a positive descriptive correlation with enterprise value growth (r = 0.165) and was statistically significant in the baseline firm-clustered regression (β = 0.847, SE = 0.295, p = 0.008; R² = 0.027; adjusted R² = 0.022), after adding EBITDA margin (β = 0.837, p = 0.013), and in the interaction specification (β = 0.791, p = 0.014). EBITDA margin (β = −0.043, p = 0.783), the revenue-growth–EBITDA interaction (β = −0.011, p = 0.287), and the stand-alone Rule of 40 (β = 0.154, p = 0.428) were insignificant. Formal pooled interaction tests did not identify significant cross-group slope differences for revenue growth (F(2, 29) = 1.281, p = 0.293), EBITDA margin (F(2, 29) = 0.251, p = 0.780), or the Rule of 40 (F(2, 29) = 1.325, p = 0.282). Among lower-revenue firms, high growth combined with a high margin was associated with median enterprise value growth of 28.8%, versus 15.9% for high growth with a low margin and −7.0% for low growth with a low margin; in the full sample, the third Rule-of-40 quartile recorded the highest median enterprise value growth of 31.6%, compared with 18.4% in the highest quartile. A direct comparison of observations with the Rule of 40 ≥ 40 versus < 40 produced no significant valuation difference (β = −4.445, p = 0.424). These findings indicate that revenue growth has the clearest contemporaneous association with enterprise-value dynamics, whereas the Rule of 40 is better interpreted as a contextual descriptive indicator than as a universal valuation threshold.</jats:p>
title: Enterprise Value Dynamics in Publicly Traded SaaS Firms: Revenue Growth, EBITDA Margin, and the Rule of 40 across Revenue-Defined Growth Stages
